_doc: Team figures: source file (inside the figures folder) -> substance, new name, title, short explanation, data type (obs = satellite observation, model = model-derived, team = dataset not stated), source, zone. 'main' marks the main photo of a substance.

figures.titre: World map of aerosol optical depth (AOT at 550 nm), mean 2004–2026
figures.explication: Dark red means a hazier sky. The darkest belt runs from the Sahara and the Sahel to the Middle East, India and eastern China: desert dust plus pollution. Oceans and the poles stay light: clean air.

figures.titre: World mean AOT, one point every 6 months (2004–2026)
figures.explication: The world average stays between about 0.128 and 0.147. It goes up and down from one semester to the next without a simple steady direction; the lowest semesters appear around 2013 and 2016.

figures.titre: Morocco mean AOT, one point every 6 months (2004–2026)
figures.explication: Morocco is roughly twice as hazy as the world average (about 0.16 to 0.30). The line zig-zags strongly: dusty semesters alternate with clearer ones, which hides any slow change.

figures.titre: Mean AOT over the Morocco window
figures.explication: The haze increases towards the south: the Saharan south and the border with Mauritania are the dustiest (red), the Mediterranean north and the Atlas are the clearest (orange).

figures.titre: Unusual semesters of world AOT (z-score, thresholds ±2)
figures.explication: Each bar compares a semester with the usual value. Bars beyond the dashed lines are exceptional. The lowest semesters (around 2012–2013 and 2016) reach the −2 line; no semester goes above +2.

figures.titre: AOT over Morocco, cells inside the borders only
figures.explication: Same map cut to Morocco's borders. The southern provinces along the Atlantic (Laâyoune to Dakhla) are the haziest; the north-west (Tangier, Rabat, Fès) is the clearest.

figures.source: Satellite methane product (dataset not stated on the figure)
figures.titre: World methane, 2004–2026
figures.explication: Methane rises almost every year, from about 1805 ppb in 2004 to about 1858 ppb in 2025. The small zig-zag is the seasonal cycle: one point every 6 months.

figures.titre: Methane statistics by semester, 2004–2016 (coverage, mean, min, max in ppb)
figures.explication: The team's table: one row per semester with the share of the grid that has data (about 79 %) and the mean methane. These numbers are used on this site for the semester analysis of methane.

figures.titre: Methane statistics by semester, 2016–2026 (continued)
figures.explication: Second part of the table, up to 2026-S1. The mean keeps rising, from about 1849 ppb in 2016-S2 to about 1873 ppb in 2026-S1.

figures.source: Satellite methane product (dataset not stated on the figure)
figures.titre: World methane with its straight-line trend
figures.explication: The orange dashed line is the best straight line through the points: the rise is steady and the points stay close to the line for 22 years.

figures.source: Satellite methane product (dataset not stated on the figure)
figures.titre: World methane compared with the 2004–2013 average
figures.explication: Below zero before about 2009, above zero afterwards and growing: recent semesters are about 40 ppb above the 2004–2013 average.

figures.source: Satellite methane product (dataset not stated on the figure)
figures.titre: Where methane increases: trend map 2004–2026 (ppb per year)
figures.explication: Red everywhere: methane increases over the whole planet, not only near its sources, because it mixes around the globe in a few months. White areas have no valid data.

figures.source: Satellite methane product (dataset not stated on the figure)
figures.titre: Methane maps for 2015, 2020, 2025 and 2026
figures.explication: Four years with the same colour scale: the colours become lighter green (higher methane) from 2015 to 2026. The northern hemisphere is always higher than the southern one.

figures.source: Satellite methane product (dataset not stated on the figure)
figures.titre: Methane over the Morocco box, 2004–2026
figures.explication: Over Morocco, methane follows the world rise: from about 1834 ppb in 2004 to about 1913 ppb in 2025, with the same 6-month zig-zag.

figures.source: Satellite methane product (dataset not stated on the figure)
figures.titre: Methane over the Morocco box in 2004, 2015 and 2026
figures.explication: Three snapshots of the same box. The colour becomes lighter from 2004 to 2026: higher methane. The white triangle is land where the product has no data.

figures.source: Satellite methane product (dataset not stated on the figure)
figures.explication: Six years side by side: the maps turn from green-blue to orange-red, showing the global increase step by step.

figures.source: Satellite methane product (dataset not stated on the figure)
figures.titre: Methane anomaly maps: 2010, 2020, 2026
figures.explication: Difference from the usual value: almost white in 2010 (normal), red in 2020, deep red in 2026. The whole map warms in colour, so the increase is global.

figures.source: Satellite methane product (dataset not stated on the figure)
figures.titre: World methane trend 2004–2026 (ppb per year)
figures.explication: The team's summary map: almost every cell is orange to red, a rise of a few ppb per year. No region shows a decrease.

figures.titre: World mean NO₂ column, 2004-10-01 to 2026-11-12
figures.explication: Red spots are where fuel is burned: eastern China, northern India, Europe, the eastern United States and the South African Highveld. Oceans are low. Very high values near the poles should be read with caution (difficult measurements there).

figures.titre: Mean NO₂ over Morocco, 2004–2026
figures.explication: The highest values are in the north-west, along the Atlantic corridor where cities, traffic and industry are concentrated. The south is low.

figures.titre: World mean NO₂, one point every 6 months
figures.explication: NO₂ stays between 2.8 and 3.1 × 10¹⁵ molecules/cm². The clear dip in 2020 matches the COVID-19 lockdowns. The very last point is high, but that semester may be incomplete.

figures.titre: NO₂ by continent, one point every 6 months
figures.explication: Asia is the highest, then Europe and North America; South America and Oceania are the lowest. Every continent shows its own 6-month rhythm.

figures.titre: NO₂ — South America
figures.explication: A strong up-and-down every 6 months: the burning season of forests and fields adds NO₂ every year, then it falls back.

figures.titre: NO₂ — Oceania
figures.explication: Low values with a slow decrease until about 2023, then a small rise. The first point (2004) is the highest of the series.

figures.titre: NO₂ — North America
figures.explication: Mostly stable around 3.4–3.6 × 10¹⁵, a low in 2020 (lockdowns), then higher values again.

figures.titre: NO₂ — Europe
figures.explication: A rise until about 2017, a clear drop in 2020–2021, then a recovery. The last point is high but may come from an incomplete semester.

figures.titre: NO₂ — Asia
figures.explication: Asia has the highest values. They rose until about 2011, then decreased slowly, with a minimum in 2020, and increased again afterwards.

figures.titre: NO₂ — Africa
figures.explication: A regular zig-zag every 6 months linked to the fire seasons north and south of the equator, with no clear long-term direction.

figures.source: Snowmelt product (dataset not stated on the figure)
figures.titre: World mean snowmelt, 2004–2026
figures.explication: Snowmelt only happens where snow falls: Canada, Alaska, Scandinavia, Siberia and the high mountains. Everywhere else the map is dark (no melt).

figures.source: Snowmelt product (dataset not stated on the figure)
figures.titre: Mean snowmelt over Morocco, 2004–2026
figures.explication: In Morocco, melt water comes from one narrow band: the High and Middle Atlas, from the south-west to the north-east. This is the water tower that feeds rivers and dams in spring.

figures.source: Snowmelt product (dataset not stated on the figure)
figures.titre: Snowmelt by continent, one point every 6 months
figures.explication: Europe and North America melt the most, with a big peak every first semester (spring) and a low every second semester. Africa stays close to zero: its melt is concentrated in the Atlas.

figures.source: Snowmelt product (dataset not stated on the figure)
figures.titre: Where snowmelt changes: trend map 2004–2026
figures.explication: Blue = less melt water over time, red = more. Eastern Canada and parts of Europe turn blue (less snow to melt); parts of the Arctic and Siberia turn red.

figures.titre: Water vapour over Morocco at 100 hPa (about 16 km high), one point every 6 months, 2004–2025
figures.explication: Grey dots are the semester anomalies, the blue line is the trend: +0.209 ppmv per decade (95 % range +0.127 to +0.292), clearly significant. The orange dashed line stops before the Hunga Tonga eruption (2022): the rise was already there before, but smaller (+0.129).

figures.titre: Map of the water-vapour trend at 100 hPa around Morocco, 2004–2025
figures.explication: Every cell is red (increase of about +0.15 to +0.22 ppmv per decade) and every cell has a black dot (significant). The black frame is the area averaged for Morocco.

figures.titre: Water-vapour trend at every altitude above Morocco
figures.explication: Read it from bottom (near 260 hPa, about 10 km) to top (0.001 hPa, about 90 km). Red dots are significant. From about 100 hPa up to about 0.05 hPa the trend is small but positive and significant; the lowest levels change a lot and are not significant.

figures.titre: Unusual semesters of water vapour over Morocco (100 hPa)
figures.explication: The grey band is the normal range (±1.5 standard deviations). Red dots are exceptionally high semesters: 2021-S2, 2022-S1, 2023-S2, 2025-S1 and 2025-S2. All are recent.

figures.titre: World water vapour at 100 hPa, one point every 6 months, 2004–2025
figures.explication: Same analysis for the whole planet: +0.178 ppmv per decade (95 % range +0.114 to +0.243), significant. Morocco rises slightly faster than the world average.

figures.titre: World map of the water-vapour trend at 100 hPa, 2004–2025
figures.explication: The whole map is red: water vapour at this altitude increases everywhere. The rise is weaker over South Asia and the western Pacific (light colours), stronger over the oceans and the high latitudes.

figures.titre: World water-vapour trend at every altitude
figures.explication: Like the Morocco profile: a small, significant increase through the stratosphere and mesosphere (red dots), and large uncertain changes in the lowest layer.

figures.titre: Unusual semesters of world water vapour (100 hPa)
figures.explication: Only two semesters are exceptionally high for the whole planet: 2023-S2 and 2025-S1, both after the Hunga Tonga eruption.

figures.titre: Where vegetation gets greener or browner: NDVI trend 2004–2026
figures.explication: Green = the land becomes greener, red = browner. Strong greening over India, China, Europe and Russia; browning patches in parts of South America, southern Africa and the western United States. Note: the colour bar shows NDVI × 10⁸ (see the note on this page).

figures.titre: World greenness (NDVI anomaly), one point every 6 months
figures.explication: The planet slowly becomes greener: the anomaly rises from below zero in 2004–2012 to above zero after 2016. The two last points jump up; the very last semester (2026-S2) has only 4 months, so it is not comparable.

figures.titre: Mean NDVI by large latitude zones
figures.explication: The tropics are always the greenest. The northern zones swing strongly every 6 months (green summer, brown or snowy winter). The last point of each line uses an incomplete semester.

figures.titre: Unusual semesters of world greenness (z-score, ±1.5)
figures.explication: Only 2026-S1 and 2026-S2 leave the grey band. 2026-S2 has only 4 months (July–October, the green season), so its high value is partly an artefact.

figures.source: Wind speed 50 m maps by the team (dataset name not written on the maps)
figures.titre: Animation: wind speed at 50 m, one map every 6 months (2004-S1 → 2026-S1)
figures.explication: The 45 semester maps of the team played one after the other. The patterns barely move from year to year: strong westerlies around 50°S, trade-wind belts over the oceans, calm continental interiors. The S1/S2 flicker is the season.

figures.source: Wind speed 50 m maps by the team (dataset name not written on the maps)
figures.titre: Wind speed at 50 m — 2004-S1 (January–June)
figures.explication: Yellow = strong wind (≥ 10 m/s), dark blue = calm. The strongest winds blow over the Southern Ocean around 50°S, along the Antarctic coast and over Greenland; continents and the equatorial forests are calm.

figures.source: Wind speed 50 m maps by the team (dataset name not written on the maps)
figures.titre: Wind speed at 50 m — 2004-S2 (July–December)
figures.explication: Second half of the year: the southern westerlies are at their strongest (southern winter) and the trade winds shift north with the season.

figures.source: Wind speed 50 m maps by the team (dataset name not written on the maps)
figures.titre: Wind speed at 50 m — 2015-S1
figures.explication: The same large-scale structure eleven years later: wind patterns are set by the planet's general circulation.

figures.source: Wind speed 50 m maps by the team (dataset name not written on the maps)
figures.titre: Wind speed at 50 m — 2026-S1
figures.explication: The latest semester of the series: the same large-scale structure.

figures.source: Irradiation SWGDN maps by the team (MERRA-2 variable name)
figures.titre: Animation: surface solar irradiation (SWGDN), one map every 6 months (2004-S1 → 2026-S1)
figures.explication: The 45 semester maps of the team played one after the other. The bright belt follows the Sun: north of the equator in S1, south in S2. The Sahara and Arabia stay among the sunniest places on Earth.

figures.source: Irradiation SWGDN maps by the team (MERRA-2 variable name)
figures.titre: Surface solar irradiation — 2004-S1 (January–June), W/m²
figures.explication: Dark red = most sunlight reaching the ground (above 250 W/m² on average day and night). The maximum is over the Sahara, Arabia and the subtropical oceans; cloudy equatorial regions and the poles receive less.

figures.source: Irradiation SWGDN maps by the team (MERRA-2 variable name)
figures.titre: Surface solar irradiation — 2004-S2 (July–December)
figures.explication: Second half of the year: the southern hemisphere receives more sunlight (its spring and summer), the northern high latitudes much less.

figures.source: Irradiation SWGDN maps by the team (MERRA-2 variable name)
figures.titre: Surface solar irradiation — 2015-S1
figures.explication: Same seasonal pattern eleven years later. Morocco sits at the edge of the sunniest belt of the planet.

figures.source: Irradiation SWGDN maps by the team (MERRA-2 variable name)
figures.titre: Surface solar irradiation — 2026-S1
figures.explication: The latest semester of the series.
